name: heavy-baritone-ledger-drawl
style: late-90s New York boom bap, 88 BPM, bare hard kick and cracking snare with wide empty gaps, one dark minor-key loop, dusty vinyl grit, a quick turntable scratch between rules, no hook. Vocal: heavy-set young Brooklyn man, deep round chest baritone, unhurried and conversational, sits a hair behind the beat yet lands every syllable dead on, faint breathy wheeze between bars, dry close-mic, punches each "Number" like a count-off
exclude: singing, melodic vocals, sung hook, choir, autotune, female vocals, trap hi-hats, 808 bass, synth pad, guitar
lyrics:
[Intro: spoken, low and close]
Uh. Uh-huh.
Money printer manual. Page one. Take notes.

[Verse: dry rap, count-off on each number]
Number one: never tell 'em what you printed,
trillions out the back door, keep the ledger tinted.

[Scratch]
Number four: never get high on your own supply,
banks took the first hit, now the rent's sky-high.

[Scratch]
Number six: no credit? Nah, they live on the slate,
and you're paying it back in the price on your plate.

[Scratch]
Number seven: keep the family out the business,
Treasury and the bank in one bed, God as my witness.

[Scratch]
Number ten: no consignment, cash up front, that's law,
they took the bailout on tick and they ain't paid at all.

[Outro: spoken, beat drops out]
And the fix, from the future? Easy.
No hand on the printer.

[End]

The voice is an older man, fifties, gravelly and smoke-scarred, who half-raps and half-talks, flat and in no hurry, like the crew's bookkeeper walking a new kid through the accounts; quiet threat, a grin leaking through on the jokes, lagging a hair behind the kick. The loop: one muted trumpet figure circling over a plucked upright bass, slow weighty dusty boom-bap drums with a dry crack on the two and four, tape hiss, a little record crackle, lots of empty space, roughly 84 bpm. For the final couplet the band stops and only the voice is left, dry.

name: noir-strings-spoken-sermon
style: mid-90s New York crime-saga hip hop, slow cinematic noir: a mournful minor-key violin phrase looping like an old detective-film score, bowed cello droning underneath, sparse dusty kick and a heavy dry snare at 82 BPM for a slow head nod, lots of air around the voice. Lead is a huge, slow, cavernous bass baritone, Brooklyn vowels, delivering each rule like a minister reading scripture, mostly talked rather than rapped, deliberate rests between lines, a dry smirk under the gravity. Each counted number lands in a big stone-church echo; the rest stays bone-dry and intimate. Chilly, patient, final.
